report:
Your assessment is correct — the best available evidence indicates that saw palmetto does **not** improve BPH symptoms beyond placebo in the longer term. Here is the key evidence:

**1. The STEP Trial (NEJM, 2006)**
This landmark one-year, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial randomized 225 men (age >49) with moderate-to-severe BPH to saw palmetto extract (160 mg twice daily) or placebo. It found that saw palmetto was **not superior to placebo** for improving urinary symptoms or objective measures such as peak urinary flow rate and prostate size.
https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJMoa053085

**2. The CAMUS Trial (JAMA, 2011)**
This larger, multicenter trial tested whether *escalating doses* of saw palmetto (up to 960 mg/day, triple the standard dose) over 72 weeks could outperform placebo in 369 men. Even at these higher doses, saw palmetto showed **no significant benefit** over placebo on AUASI symptom scores or other outcomes.
https://jamanetwork.com/journals/jama/fullarticle/1104439

**3. Cochrane Systematic Review (2012)**
Tacklind et al. updated the Cochrane review of *Serenoa repens* monotherapy for BPH. Incorporating the newer, higher-quality trials, the review concluded that saw palmetto was **not superior to placebo** for improving lower urinary tract symptoms, a shift from earlier, more optimistic conclusions based on smaller, methodologically weaker studies.
https://www.cochranelibrary.com/cdsr/doi/10.1002/14651858.CD002281.pub3/full

**4. NCCIH (NIH)**
The U.S. National Center for Complementary and Integrative Health states that saw palmetto has **not been shown to be effective** for BPH, citing the STEP and CAMUS trials as pivotal negative evidence.
https://www.nccih.nih.gov/health/saw-palmetto

**Conclusion:** Two large, rigorous, long-term RCTs and an updated Cochrane review consistently show no meaningful benefit of saw palmetto over placebo for BPH symptoms. Earlier positive findings came from smaller, lower-quality trials. Your conclusion of "no" is well-supported.
